rendered: NFA hydroxide precursors must be coprecipitated within a narrow pH window, between 10 and 12[1] (pH units). The reason is that nickel, iron and aluminum ions have different solubility products, so simultaneous coprecipitation is difficult. Aluminum hydroxide starts precipitating at a lower pH than nickel hydroxide, while nickel and iron hydroxides precipitate only beyond pH 6[2]. This shifts the usable window, and the lower limit is held by the reactor control: NaOH is pumped in to maintain the pH to above 10[3], especially for nickel-rich materials. Precursors are made in a continuous stirred tank reactor fed with metal sulfates, carbonates, or chlorides and a chelating agent[4] (for example NH4OH), with pH, temperature and stirring speed controlled. The outflow from the reactor is filtered, washed, and dried[5] to obtain the hydroxide precursors. These are mixed with a lithium source (Li2CO3, LiOH, LiNO3, etc.[6]) and calcined in an O2-rich environment at temperatures above 600[7] °C. After calcination, the NFA cathode powders were cast into[8] electrodes using a roll-to-roll slot-die coating process[9], followed by pouch cell assembly.
